name: Wheat
summary: Wheat is hardly grown in the Philippines, and nearly all the wheat for bread and noodles comes from abroad. A few highland growers and hobby farmers raise small plots in the cool dry months, and this short guide shows how they do it.
season: In the highlands, small plots are sown at the end of the rains, around October to December, so the crop grows through the cool, dry months and ripens before the summer rains. Lowland heat gives weak plants and poor heads.
material: Dry seed, usually brought in from abroad or shared among growers. It is sown dry without soaking.
spacing: Rows about 20 to 25 cm apart with seed sown thinly, or broadcast evenly over the plot.
water: Grown on the last of the rains and watered by hand or by hose on small plots during dry spells.
fertilizer: Compost or manure with some complete fertilizer (14 14 14) at sowing and a light dose of urea (46 0 0) at tillering.
care: Hand weeding in the first month and guarding the heads from birds. Rust is the main disease in warm, damp weather.
harvest: Ready in about 100 to 120 days, when the straw is golden and the grain is hard. Cut by sickle, sun dried, threshed by beating and winnowed.

ways.label: Sown direct in rows or broadcast

steps.title: Dig or plow to a fine bed
steps.how: Plow or dig the plot, remove the weeds and rake it to a fine, level bed.

steps.title: Sow the seed
steps.how: Sow the seed thinly in shallow rows about 20 to 25 cm apart and cover it with 3 to 5 cm of soil, or scatter it evenly and rake it in.

steps.title: Fertilizer at sowing
steps.how: Mix compost or manure and some complete fertilizer (14 14 14) into the rows at sowing.

steps.title: Water if dry
steps.how: Water the plot if no rain falls, so the seed comes up evenly.

steps.title: Weed
steps.how: Hand pull the weeds while the plants are young.

steps.title: Urea at tillering
steps.how: Give a light side dressing of urea (46 0 0) as the plants start to tiller.

steps.title: Watch for rust and birds
steps.how: Look for orange or brown rust spots on the leaves, and guard the ripening heads from birds.

steps.title: Cut when golden and dry
steps.how: Harvest when the straw is golden and the grain is hard. Cut with a sickle and tie in bundles.

steps.title: Dry and thresh
steps.how: Dry the bundles in the sun, then beat them to free the grain, winnow and dry the grain before storing.

mistakes: Planting in the lowlands or in the rainy season, when heat and wet weather ruin the heads.
Sowing too thickly, which gives thin stems that fall over.
Harvesting late in the rains, so grain sprouts or molds in the head.
better: Get seed of a variety bred for warm climates.
Sow only in the cool dry months in the highlands.
Test the soil and lime it if it is acid.
Keep the plot weed free for the first month.

watering.traditional: The few wheat plots in our highlands are sown at the end of the rains and live on the last of the rain. Growers water small plots by hand or by hose during dry spells.
watering.method: Hand watering with a can or a hose on small plots, in the morning.
watering.rainfed: Sow at the end of the rains, from October to December, while the soil is still moist, so the crop grows on stored moisture through the cool months.
watering.dryseason: The crop grows through the dry months, so water small plots about once a week in dry spells, more at heading and flowering, and stop once the grain hardens.
watering.wet: Wet, warm weather brings rust and rotting heads. Plant on beds that drain, and do not sow so early that the heads come out in the rains.

schedule.often: Water the plot right after sowing and every few days if no rain falls
schedule.amount: Enough to moisten the seed rows, never soggy
schedule.why: The seed needs even moisture to come up together.

schedule.often: In dry spells, water about once a week
schedule.amount: Soak the rows with a can or a hose
schedule.why: Moisture now gives more shoots and more heads.

schedule.often: Keep the soil moist, watering when the topsoil dries
schedule.amount: A good soaking of the rows
schedule.why: Drought now gives short heads with empty spaces.

schedule.often: Water in dry spells until the grain is firm

schedule.why: The straw and grain must dry for cutting.

critical: Tillering, about day 10 to 45: dry soil means fewer heads.
Heading, flowering and grain filling, about day 45 to 100: a dry spell gives light, shriveled grain.

signs.dry: Leaves roll and turn gray green, the plants stay short with few shoots, and the heads are small.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves, rust spots and moldy heads.

better: Water at tillering and at heading if you can water only twice.
A light mulch between the rows keeps the topsoil moist longer.
